CKD with acute on chronic; differentiate by chronic stigmata (small kidneys on US, persistent proteinuria).

faq.a: Nephron loss leads to fibrosis and shrinkage; the remaining nephrons hypertrophy but overall renal length decreases.
faq.q: Why are kidneys small in chronic disease?

faq.a: No; size reduction reflects irreversible structural loss, though function may stabilize with treatment.
faq.q: Can a small kidney be reversible?

faq.a: Clinical clues (long‑standing hypertension, proteinuria, low eGFR) plus physical exam (small flank dullness) suggest chronic disease.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with uncontrolled hypertension presents with serum creatinine 180 µmol/L and kidneys 8 cm on US. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — Hypertensive nephrosclerosis; start ACE‑I/ARB and arrange 3‑monthly eGFR monitoring.

A patient with HIV on tenofovir develops eGFR 35 mL/min/1.73 m² and small kidneys. Which drug should be reconsidered and why? — Tenofovir; it is nephrotoxic and may accelerate tubular injury, switch to a safer regimen.
How does tubulointerstitial TB cause small kidneys and what test confirms it when microscopy is negative? — Granulomatous inflammation leads to fibrosis; urine GeneXpert or PCR provides confirmation.
What blood pressure target is recommended in CKD with small kidneys and why? — < 130/80 mmHg to reduce further nephron loss and proteinuria.

A patient with CKD stage 4 presents with potassium 6.2 mmol/L and ECG changes. What immediate management is required? — Urgent potassium‑lowering measures (calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, nebulised β2‑agonist) and arrange dialysis if refractory.
Explain why a normal serum creatinine does not rule out CKD in a malnourished woman with small kidneys on US. — Low muscle mass lowers creatinine production; rely on eGFR, imaging and proteinuria.
Which antihypertensive class is contraindicated in a CKD patient with hyperkalaemia and why? — ACE‑I/ARB; they reduce potassium excretion and can worsen hyperkalaemia.

Distinguish chronic obstruction from chronic parenchymal disease on ultrasound. — Obstruction shows hydronephrosis with dilated pelvis; chronic disease shows uniformly small, echogenic kidneys without dilation.
ai.title: Small Kidneys
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Small kidneys on imaging indicate chronic kidney disease, often from long‑standing hypertension, diabetes, or tubulointerstitial disease. In low‑resource settings, infections such as TB and HIV are common causes. Recognising the pattern guides staging, management and referral.

b: Ultrasound measurement of bipolar length
Absence of hydronephrosis or cystic lesions
sections.p: Renal length < 9 cm in adults (or < 2 SD below age‑matched mean) on ultrasound defines a small kidney. It reflects irreversible loss of nephrons and chronic disease.

t.b: What is the renal size and structural pattern? – Confirms small kidneys and excludes obstruction or cystic disease
What is the current kidney function? – Determines CKD stage; low eGFR with small kidneys supports chronicity
Is there proteinuria? – Persistent proteinuria suggests glomerular disease as a cause

b: eGFR 45‑59 → CKD 3a
eGFR 30‑44 → CKD 3b
eGFR 15‑29 → CKD 4
eGFR < 15 → CKD 5
sections.p: Stage CKD by eGFR (KDIGO): 3a 45‑59, 3b 30‑44, 4 15‑29, 5 < 15 mL/min/1.73 m². Small kidneys usually appear from stage 3 onward.

b: 1. Hypertensive nephrosclerosis – long‑standing uncontrolled BP
2. Diabetic nephropathy – common in urban centres
3. Tubulointerstitial disease – TB, HIV, schistosomiasis
4. Chronic glomerulonephritis – post‑streptococcal, lupus
5. Herbal nephrotoxicity – traditional remedies
sections.p: In East African low‑resource hospitals the hierarchy is:

b: Persistent hypertension resistant to ≥2 drugs
Gradual rise in serum creatinine over months
Proteinuria (often < 1 g/day in tubulointerstitial disease)
Hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis in stage 4‑5
sections.p: Patients often have insidious fatigue, reduced urine output, and hypertension. Advanced disease shows oedema, uremic symptoms, and electrolyte disturbances.
Prioritise tests that confirm chronicity, identify a treatable cause and guide management.

t.b: Are potassium and bicarbonate deranged? – Guides need for dialysis or urgent correction
Is HIV infection present? – Positive result points to HIV‑associated nephropathy
Is there TB involvement of the kidney? – Positive result directs anti‑TB therapy
Is there sterile pyuria or casts? – Sterile pyuria suggests TB; granular casts suggest tubulointerstitial disease
Is hypertension uncontrolled? – Determines need for intensified antihypertensive regimen

b: Uremic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis)
Severe hyperkalaemia > 6.0 mmol/L
Metabolic acidosis bicarbonate < 15 mmol/L
Pulmonary oedema or refractory fluid overload
Rapid rise in creatinine > 30 % in 2 weeks
sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent referral or dialysis.

b: ACE inhibitor or ARB – first‑line for hypertension and proteinuria; avoid if potassium > 5.5 mmol/L or creatinine rises > 30 %
Loop diuretic – for volume overload; monitor electrolytes
Low‑potassium diet & bicarbonate supplementation – correct hyperkalaemia and acidosis
Anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) when TB confirmed – prevents further renal loss
Antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir‑sparing if possible) for HIV‑associated disease – reduces progression
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control BP, manage electrolytes and plan renal replacement when indicated.

b: eGFR and electrolytes every 3‑6 months
BP at each visit, target < 130/80 mmHg
Urine protein annually
Vaccination against hepatitis B and pneumococcus
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, high‑dose aminoglycosides)
sections.p: Regular monitoring slows progression and detects complications early.

b: Hydronephrosis – dilated collecting system, usually unilateral, treatable surgically
Renal cystic disease – enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts
Acute kidney injury – kidneys may be normal size; history of rapid creatinine rise
sections.p: Conditions that can mimic small kidneys on imaging or present similarly.

b: Normal serum creatinine in early CKD with low muscle mass – rely on eGFR and ultrasound
Proteinuria absent in tubulointerstitial disease – look for granular casts instead
Negative urine TB smear does not exclude renal TB – consider GeneXpert or PCR
